package_info.package_manager: Linux binary (Mirai-variant botnet, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The Condi botnet is a Mirai-variant DDoS malware that propagates by exploiting router vulnerabilities (notably CVE-2023-1389), deletes critical system binaries to prevent remediation, kills competing malware and system processes, establishes C2 communication, and launches DDoS attacks. It also hosts and updates its own binaries, and attempts to persist by deleting system shutdown/reboot binaries, making removal difficult without a power cycle.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code deletes system binaries responsible for rebooting or shutting down the device, removing administrator ability to perform system management operations, resulting in malware persistence until a physical power cycle.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting core system management binaries is a deliberate attempt to prevent administrators from rebooting or shutting down the device, thereby hindering malware removal.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software should never delete or tamper with essential system binaries required for device management.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In rare cases, embedded systems may remove unused binaries to save space, but never critical system management tools.
key_indicators: Deletes critical system binaries (reboot, shutdown, poweroff, halt)
Targets multiple standard locations for these binaries

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Reads /proc/<PID>/status for each running process and compares the Name field to a list of strings (e.g., /bin/busybox, /bin/systemd, /usr/bin, test, /tmp/condi, /tmp/zxcr9999, /var/condibot, etc.), then kills matching processes.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates all running processes, compares their names to a blacklist of known competing malware and system process names, and terminates any matching processes, thereby eliminating competition and disrupting system operation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Killing processes based on a static blacklist is a common malware technique to remove other malware and evade detection, and can also disrupt legitimate system processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not indiscriminately terminate unrelated processes, especially those critical to system operation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Security software may terminate known malware, but not in such an indiscriminate or self-serving manner.
key_indicators: Kills processes by matching against a hardcoded blacklist
Targets both malware and legitimate system process names

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Kills any process with a binary filename containing architecture-specific extensions (x86, x86_64, arm, arm5, arm6, arm7, mips, mipsel, sh4, ppc).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code scans running processes for binary filenames containing architecture-specific substrings and terminates those processes, aiming to remove other botnets or malware that use such naming conventions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This broad and aggressive process-killing method is designed to eliminate competing malware, but can also disrupt legitimate processes that happen to match the pattern.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not kill processes based on architecture-specific substrings in their filenames.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; this is a malware-specific anti-competition technique.
key_indicators: Kills processes by matching architecture-specific substrings in filenames
Targets common architecture names (x86, arm, mips, etc.)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Generates a random string of at least ten characters from a custom alphanumeric set and attempts to kill any process with this string in its command line.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code generates a random alphanumeric string and attempts to terminate any process whose command line contains this string, though this is unlikely to match any real process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This appears to be a flawed or incomplete anti-competition feature, possibly intended to target specific malware, but implemented in a way that is ineffective.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not attempt to kill processes based on random strings.
key_indicators: Attempts to kill processes using randomly generated command line substrings
Uses a custom character set for string generation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Generates two random numbers (one between 12 and 32, another between 12 and 20) and kills any process with a command line length matching either number.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code generates two random numbers within specified ranges and terminates any process whose command line length matches either value, potentially disrupting legitimate system processes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is a highly destructive and indiscriminate technique that can kill legitimate system processes, causing device instability or failure.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate software kills processes based on command line length.
key_indicators: Kills processes by matching random command line lengths

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Scans public IPs for open ports 80 or 8080, then sends a hardcoded exploitation request to download and execute a remote shell script from hxxp://cdn2[.]duc3k[.]com/t.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime after infection, the code scans public IP addresses for open HTTP ports (80 or 8080), sends exploitation requests targeting CVE-2023-1389, and downloads and executes a remote shell script from a hardcoded malicious URL to propagate the malware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated exploitation and remote code execution for self-propagation is a hallmark of worm and botnet malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not scan the internet for vulnerable devices or execute remote shell scripts without explicit authorization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may perform similar actions, but only with explicit authorization and in controlled environments.
key_indicators: Automated scanning for open HTTP ports (80, 8080)
Downloads and executes remote shell scripts from hardcoded URLs

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Upon receiving a C2 command (\x33\x66\x66), downloads bot binaries from a hardcoded IP and port, then starts a basic HTTP server on a random port above 1024 to host these binaries. Responds to GET/POST/HEAD requests for /arm, /arm7, /mips, /mipsel, /x86_64, /sh4, /ppc, /m68k with the corresponding binaries.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after receiving a specific C2 command, the code downloads updated malware binaries from a hardcoded IP and port, then starts a local HTTP server on a random high port, masquerading as Apache, to serve these binaries for further propagation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hosting and serving malware binaries is a core propagation technique for botnets, and masquerading as Apache is intended to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not download and serve malware binaries or impersonate well-known HTTP servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software update servers may serve binaries, but not in this context or with this intent.
key_indicators: Downloads and serves malware binaries via local HTTP server
Uses random high ports for hosting

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Implements multiple DDoS attack functions: attack_tcp_syn, attack_tcp_ack, attack_tcp_socket, attack_tcp_thread, attack_tcp_bypass, attack_udp_plain, attack_udp_thread, attack_udp_smart.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after receiving attack commands from C2, the code launches various DDoS attacks (TCP SYN, ACK, UDP floods, etc.) against specified targets, generating high volumes of malicious network traffic.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching DDoS attacks is inherently malicious and illegal, and the presence of multiple attack vectors indicates a sophisticated botnet.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate software should launch network floods against arbitrary targets.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may simulate DDoS, but only in controlled, authorized environments.
key_indicators: Implements multiple DDoS attack vectors (TCP SYN, ACK, UDP, etc.)
Receives attack parameters from C2 server

attack_chain.action: Malware is delivered to a vulnerable TP-Link router via exploitation of CVE-2023-1389 (or other vulnerabilities).
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial infection and execution of the malware binary

attack_chain.action: Malware deletes system management binaries to prevent reboot/shutdown and attempts to kill competing malware and system processes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and exclusive control of the infected device

attack_chain.action: Malware establishes C2 communication and registers itself, awaiting further instructions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ready to receive C2 commands for propagation or attack

attack_chain.action: Upon C2 command, malware downloads updated binaries and starts a local HTTP server to serve them, masquerading as Apache.
attack_chain.leads_to: Facilitates further propagation to new devices

attack_chain.action: Upon C2 command, malware launches DDoS attacks against specified targets using various attack methods.

behavioral_signatures: Deletion of system management binaries (reboot, shutdown, poweroff, halt) from standard locations
Process termination based on hardcoded name blacklists, architecture-specific filename substrings, random command line substrings, or command line length
Automated scanning of public IPs for open HTTP ports (80, 8080) and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2023-1389
Hosting and serving malware binaries via a local HTTP server masquerading as Apache on random high ports
Receiving and executing DDoS attack commands from C2, resulting in high-volume network floods
file_indicators: Temporary files or binaries named after architectures (arm, mips, x86, etc.)
network_indicators: C2 protocol traffic with initial bytes \x33\x66\x99
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for deletion or tampering of system management binaries (reboot, shutdown, poweroff, halt) in standard locations, and for unusual process termination activity based on process name, filename substring, or command line length. Detect outbound connections to known malicious domains or IPs (cdn2.duc3k.com, 85.217.144.35), and look for local HTTP servers masquerading as Apache on non-standard ports. Network monitoring should include detection of scanning activity for open HTTP ports, C2 protocol signatures (e.g., initial bytes \x33\x66\x99), and high-volume DDoS attack traffic originating from the device.
